subject: tinRobot
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: wind-up robot with key in its back.
Style: 1950s Japanese tin toy.
reasoning:
I'm envisioning a classic 1950s Japanese wind-up tin toy robot — boxy lithographed body with rivets, a dial-covered chest panel, round antenna head, grille mouth, cylindrical limbs with claw hands, flat feet, and a key in the back — sized like an actual small toy around a quarter meter tall.

Now I'm working out the humanoid rig: hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, arms with shoulder/elbow/wrist/finger joints, legs with hip/knee/ankle, and a hinge joint for the wind-up key. I'm settling on a total height of 0.30 meters and designing the legs as simple straight tin tubes with flat rectangular feet, building the chain from hip to ankle for the sweep geometry.

For the torso I'm planning a slightly tapered box painted like classic tin lithograph — a chest panel with rivets, seams, and dials using the clockwork kit's panelled texture and a gauge texture for a nice dial effect, plus glowing eyes and an antenna bulb using the glow helper.

Shoulders will be disc-like cylinders with side rivets, arms built as ribbed tubes (stacked lathe rings) ending in claw hands. I'm leaning toward simple pincer claws with two prongs rather than full multi-digit fingers, keeping the pose slightly out from the body in a relaxed A-pose.

For the head, I'm going with a boxy shape with a domed cap, side ear discs with bolts, and a short ribbed collar neck connecting it to the shoulders.

The face needs an antenna with a ball tip, glowing round eyes with rims, and a two-part mouth—an upper jaw with teeth and a lower jaw grille with vertical bars for a robotic look. Now I'm working out the overall proportions, starting from the foot box dimensions and building up the coordinate system for each part.

Working from ankle to hip, I'm defining leg tube radius and knee position, then the pelvis and hip joint placement, followed by the torso's barrel-shaped taper with spine joints at increasing heights, and finally the neck and head box dimensions stacking up to roughly 0.365m total.

Continuing upward, I'm adding the dome top and antenna to bring total height near 0.42 — a tall, chunky toy proportion. Now I'm working out arm placement: shoulders set wide at y=0.232, with elbow and wrist positions angled forward and down so the forearm juts out like a toy robot reaching to grab something, with claw-like fingers extending forward from the wrist.

I'm settling on roughly 0.4 units tall overall, comparable to a classic 1950s tin toy robot around 30cm. For the paint scheme, I'm thinking of the lithographed look of those vintage tin robots — a red-orange body, silver-blue head, yellow accents, keeping texel density high since the painted areas are small.

Now I'm refining the specific color assignments: red torso, steel-blue silver head, silver-grey ribbed limbs, blue feet, yellow accent details, and adding the lithograph character with pinstripes, rivets, panel seams, and folded tab edges, plus "ROBOT" text on the chest plate and "MADE IN JAPAN" stamped on the back or foot for authenticity.

I'm writing a tin paint helper function that simulates worn metal using noise-based mottling, directional lighting with lighter top and darker bottom shading, and silvery edge wear where the surface noise is highest, pulling noise, mix, smoothstep, and paint utilities from the SDK. Now I'm planning the texture set, starting with a chest panel SVG featuring dial gauges, knobs, lights, and a "ROBOT" label, followed by round glowing eye decals styled like glass lamp windows with crosshair details.

I'm sketching out the rest of the texture list: a mouth grille with black bars and teeth, a back plate with a keyhole boss, "MADE IN JAPAN" text and wind-up arrows with rivets, foot sole stripes, ear speaker grilles with concentric rings, a hazard-striped belt/pelvis band, a clockwork gauge texture, a star emblem for the shoulder disc, and an antenna ball. I'm also thinking through how to apply these textures to the geometry, favoring planes positioned on flat faces like the torso front rather than relying on box UV mapping, since decals work better on flat surfaces.

I decide decal projection is actually the cleaner approach -- using a decal function to apply textures directly onto curved or boxy surfaces by specifying position, direction, and size, which handles the projection correctly even on tapered parts like the torso. I plan to use decals for everything on the torso and head, keeping transparency and alpha cutouts intact, and I'll add a subtle glow only to specific decals like the eyes and lamps rather than lighting up the whole chest panel.

For the torso itself, I'm working out the geometry using a tapered box shape running vertically along a bone, figuring out width versus depth orientation, and painting it with a panelled texture to get a tin-like grid look. I'm also deciding which spine joint the torso bone should attach to.

Now I'm mapping out the skeleton chain structure: a hips-to-chest spine path with intermediate joints, followed by a separate neck chain extending upward from the chest point, working out the joint names and positions for each span.

Then I'm placing the head joint above the neck, calculating dimensions for the head box, dome, and antenna so the proportions stay consistent with the overall robot's larger scale.

Now I'm laying out the full joint hierarchy: hips as the root spine joint, a spine chain feeding into the neck chain, the head attached to the top neck joint, and a jaw joint hinging near the head's base.

For the jaw itself, I'm splitting the head into an upper cranium and a lower jaw box with a chin, hinged at the back-bottom and facing forward.

The jaw sits over the neck collar, with the neck top at 0.29 and radius 0.025 fitting beneath the jaw box. For the eyes, I'll place them on the upper head front at x ±0.027, y 0.348, z 0.004.

Designing the eye assembly: a chrome bezel cylinder, an amber glowing lens flattened sphere behind it, and a pupil decal on a circle plane in front for detail.

I'm skipping a nose and instead adding a brow bar strip with rivets above the eyes for character. For the mouth, I'm planning a grille texture on the jaw front with dark vertical slots instead of modeling individual teeth boxes.

For ears I'm adding small speaker-disc cylinders on each side of the head with a concentric-ring texture and a bolt detail. Now I'm reconsidering the head shape itself -- a flat box dome looks wrong for a classic tin-robot look, so I want to round it off into more of a Robby-style dome instead.

For the dome I'll keep it a shallow flattened cap with a seam ring sitting atop the boxy head, and give it an antenna rod rising from the top with a glowing red ball tip, plus a small coil spring near the base for charm. Then I'm moving on to the chest, planning a raised rectangular panel with dials as the central front detail.

I'm designing the chest panel SVG now: a cream plate bordered with rivets, a red "ROBOT" banner across the top, rows of colored round buttons below, a speaker slot, and a functional gauge dial placed over a dark recessed circle on the left side of the layout.

On the right side, I'm adding three small glowing dome lamps (red, yellow, green) as separate parts beside the gauge. I'm also detailing the torso's tin-toy character with small folded seam tabs at the corners and a hazard-striped belt band around the hips.

Now I'm adding a gold buckle disc with a star decal in the belt's center, then building out the shoulders as small cylinders with star emblem decals and tiny bolt rings, before defining the arm chain from shoulder through elbow to wrist.

For the arms I'm sweeping tubes along the shoulder-elbow-wrist path using a sinusoidal ripple radius to create a corrugated, low-poly tubing look, painted in silver tin with lighter accent rings, then adding red sphere knobs at the elbows and yellow cylindrical cuffs at the wrists.

Now for the hands I'm designing pincer-style claws: each finger is a two-joint chain with a thin flat tapered box section, curving forward from the wrist. I'm setting up base offsets at the wrist for a top-and-bottom prong pair plus an inner thumb, with curved paths so the digits angle toward each other.

Three fingers times two hands gives 18 finger joints, and tallying everything -- hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, arms, legs, plus accessories -- puts the total skeleton around 45 joints.

Setting up the legs now: hip joints positioned symmetrically, chained through knee to ankle with a slight forward bend, three points forming hipL/kneeL/ankleL with the "leg" role and a contact point at the ankle. I'm giving the leg tubes a corrugated sweep with ribs, a sphere at the knee...

Now I'm designing the foot — a tin-shoe shape with a boxy base, defining the side-profile outline with heel rising at the back and a rounded toe cap, then extruding it along the width axis to give it thickness.

I'll add a yellow ankle strap band and think through the ankle joint bone placement for the foot extrusion. For the hero feature, I want a classic wind-up key on the back — a stem rod extending outward with a butterfly-style key plate made of two rounded loop wings, attached via a dedicated key joint.

Still shaping the key outline...

I'm thinking of adding a two-tone rim effect with a slightly smaller inset extrude, plus small dark disc "holes" on each wing to suggest a hollowed bow-tie look. I'm also considering rotating the key slightly off-axis for a more charming resting pose rather than keeping it perfectly horizontal.

Simpler: I'll build all parts first, then rotate the whole key joint about its own stem axis by around 25 degrees so everything attached rides along with it. For the structure, I'm laying out the back plate as a lathed gold disc, a cylindrical stem, a collar ring, and the key head on top, possibly with a small engraved tag detail on the back plate.

Now I'm placing the wind-up key boss into the torso's back plate at its z-position, and designing the neck as a ribbed trapezoid frustum made with a lathe profile that includes three ridges, connected to the neck bone, plus a trapezoid ledge detail where the torso top lip meets the collar.

Also planning the belt zone with hazard stripes and a buckle, the silver pelvis box connecting to the legs, and front/side details like a lithographed decal panel, rivet columns, and slit-style vent textures on the torso sides.

I'm also sketching the back decal with "MADE IN JAPAN" / "WIND UP" text and the key, then listing out all needed textures: panel, gauge, eye crosshair, grille, teeth, ear speaker rings, shoulder emblem, back tag, side vents, and painted belt stripes, while deciding to skip extras like the key-wing decal and foot sole labels for now.

For part count, I'm aiming for roughly 200 pieces by adding rivets using small hemisphere geometry through a helper function, placed around the head, shoulders, ears, and knees individually rather than merged, since the total stays well under the 1000-part budget. I'm also planning to compute torso surface positions manually from known box dimensions instead of using surface-hit calculations, since the torso is a simple frustum shape.

I'm working out how decals and rivets should seat onto the slanted torso surface using ray-based hit detection against the torso part, where the hit normal automatically determines the decal's orientation and rivets stick flush along that normal. Setting up these helper functions now...

Decals should default to world up for orientation on most faces. Now defining color palettes for the tin paint job, with a tinting function that mixes base colors with highlights and shading based on surface normal lighting.

Still writing paint function...

Edge-wear detection isn't feasible without actual edge data, so I'll fake it with layered noise to create chip-like scratches showing silver underneath, plus a warm-top/cool-bottom gradient for depth. Panelled surfaces should inherit this tin paint as their base before resolving panel grid details.

Thinking through toy-scale proportions: panel size around 0.06-0.07 with small rivets (0.015-0.016) and thin seams, checking that torso width divides evenly into panel counts. For the head, I'll keep it simpler with a lighter silver tin color and minimal or no rivets.

Settling on a color palette: silvery tin for metal, red, blue for hands/feet, and yellow as accent colors.

Rounding out the palette with cream, black, a gilt metal for the gold key, and glow colors (amber, red, green) for lamp effects. For limbs, I'm using the corrugated silver tin look with a sine-based ripple function to vary the sweep radius along the arms and legs, aiming for a rippled metallic texture with roughly 8-11 cycles depending on limb length.

I'm now reconsidering whether a smooth tube with stacked torus rings along the limb path would look more reliable than the sine ripple, since placing small torus segments at intervals gives cleaner, more controllable corrugation even though it adds more parts to the build.

Actually, simpler to use flat cylinder discs as ribs since their default +Y axis already aligns with the frame's tangent, avoiding extra orientation params. I'll write a helper that walks along the chain placing these rib discs at each point...

Now I'm moving to the shoulder construction, placing a cylinder along the x-axis for the shoulder joint, then adding a flat circle decal on the outer face as an emblem, positioning it slightly offset outward to avoid z-fighting.

Working out the shoulder-to-torso connection with a short stem cylinder to bridge the gap, then defining the arm chain positions for shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints to set up the hanging arm pose.

Working out wrist and hand placement per side, computing the forearm direction vector to orient the hand naturally, and planning a cuff cylinder at the wrist to cap the sleeve.

Now I'm positioning the palm block oriented along the hand direction, then figuring out finger placement for a simple pincer claw—two prongs separated across a perpendicular axis so they face each other to grip, rather than stacking vertically.

Defining finger curve paths...

Still defining finger chains...

For legs, I'm specifying the hip chain parent and planning the parts: ribs, a knee sphere, an ankle band cylinder, and a foot extrusion from the ankle bone, with a hip socket sphere and small disc shapes near the hip joint.

For the head, I'm setting all parts to the head bone except the jaw, and working out head dimensions like width, depth, and the upper head's vertical span centered around the head joint position.

I'm adjusting the upper head's bottom boundary to fit the jaw region, and then enlarging the head dome slightly so the eyes, brow strip, and teeth decal all fit proportionally: eyes centered near y=0.345 with a small radius, a thin brow strip just above them, and a teeth line positioned just below.

I'm computing the front z-offsets so the head and jaw boxes align flush, and considering whether to use plain box geometry with silver paint for crispness, or an extruded shape with beveled edges for a more rounded tin-toy look.

Extruding outlines with chamfered corners...

I'll write a `slabBox` helper that builds a centered rectangular extrusion from an outline and thickness. Then I'm planning the ears as speaker discs with a yellow bezel ring on the head sides, and starting on the antenna with a base cylinder, stem rod, and coil on top of the dome.

For the dome itself, I'm using a lathe revolution from a profile that curves from the axis outward and back, giving a rounded red cap on top of the head to contrast with the silver body, segmented at 12 for smoothness.

Now I'm working on the neck as a ribbed lathe collar, defining a profile with alternating in-and-out radii to create the ridged look, positioning it between roughly 0.252 and 0.292 to fit inside the jaw gap, and planning to generate the ribs programmatically rather than hand-coding each point.

Next I'm shifting to the torso layout, figuring out panel placements relative to the chest's x and y bounds, with the belt covering the lower region and a chest plate centered higher up, plus a row of small lamp elements positioned just above the belt line.

Still planning the panel layout...

On the right I'll add two knobs with tick pointers and some slot lines beneath, plus side vent decals on the torso and a back label reading "MADE IN JAPAN / WIND UP" near the key hole.

For the key itself, I'm setting up a lathe-turned gold boss at the back hit point, extruding a stem into the body, and building a bow shape at the end, all attached via a joint parented to the spine for proper articulation.

For the key wings, I'm layering gold and red enamel: a base gold plate with a thin red inset outline layered on top to mimic the decorative pattern, with the bow rotation handled by posing the bone afterward.

Now I'm moving to the gauge and panel: adding a voltage dial decal with a needle, and building the panel as a thin cream-colored extruded plate with the gauge texture decaled onto its surface.

Since the torso front is flat, I realize I can simplify by using plane geometries for most flat surfaces instead of ray-casting onto curved ones, reserving decal rays only for the slanted sides where x varies with y. This keeps things deterministic and fast across torso, head, and jaw fronts.

Now I'm figuring out the belt geometry as a slab positioned just below the torso, sized slightly wider and shallower than the torso's bottom edge, with stripe decoration to paint onto it.

I'm positioning the pelvis box in darker silver beneath the torso, then working out the vertical alignment for hips, legs, ankles, and feet so each joint connects cleanly along the chain path.

Setting ankle y to 0.042, foot heel top to 0.036, and the ankle band to 0.041, I'm sizing the leg segments (hip, knee, ankle) to keep them short and chunky, matching the proportions of a classic tin-toy robot where the legs are notably shorter than the torso and head.

Now I'm moving to the SVG texture decals, starting with the eye: an amber glowing lens with a dark pupil, highlight, and thin crosshair lines overlaid for a mechanical sensor look.

I'll place the pupil circle just in front of the lens surface, giving it a dark pupil with a white highlight rather than a glow, so the eye reads as realistic rather than purely luminous. Then I'll move on to sizing the jaw grille plane to roughly match the jaw's front dimensions.

Now I'm sketching the grille as a dark rounded rect with vertical silver bars recessed into it, the teeth strip as a row of cream rectangles outlined on a dark band, and the ear as concentric rings with a yellow center bolt, each mapped onto its corresponding plane geometry.

I'm also drawing the emblem as a star on a layered yellow-red circle for shoulders and buckle, a yellow back-tag plate with rounded black border and "WIND-UP ROBOT" / "MADE IN JAPAN" text plus curved arrow accents, and a side vent made of five dark horizontal slots, while skipping hand texture and adding minor heel stripe details for the foot.

Skipping the sole label, I'm setting up the jaw as a hinge joint parented to the head, built from a slab jaw box, grille plane, chin plate, and lip tab, with small hinge bolt spheres placed near the jaw rear sides.

Now I'm sketching the rig: a head joint pointing upward and a jaw joint aimed toward a target, tagged with their respective roles. I'm importing the builder utilities and the clockwork and glow kits to start writing the actual construction code, checking that the module paths and loose TypeScript typing will compile cleanly.

I'll avoid unused imports since the typechecker rejects those, and I'm setting up basic helper constants—a builder instance, a vector type alias, a mirroring array, and a side-label function. Now I'm writing a tin paint function that mixes dark and light tones based on surface normal and layers in chipped-scratch noise for a worn metal look.

Writing plate helper...

Now I'm drafting a rivet helper using a shared low-poly sphere geometry, parameterized by position, direction, radius, and color.

Since the SDK might mutate shared geometry, I'll create fresh geometry instances each time rather than sharing across meshes—safer and cheap enough. For lamp domes I'll use a small sphere with glow, then move on to defining the joint hierarchy starting with the hips joint position and role.

Adding spine, neck, and head joints and chains...

I'll put torso/shoulders/back/key on chest (spine.joints[1]) and belt on spine1. Now I'm defining the color palette (silver, red, blue, yellow, cream, black, amber) and setting up paint materials for each part.

Still writing paint definitions...

Still adjusting flange and vent placements...

Working out the gauge plane's position, converting the SVG circle coordinates to model space while accounting for the left-right flip between viewer and model orientation, and figuring out how the plane's local axes map to world axes for proper aiming.

Three lamps (red, amber, green) sit as small glowing domes with bezels, positioned to clear the belt and panel edges. For the back decal, I'm placing the TAG plane facing -Z, which flips the local u-axis to world -X, so I need to work out which side the viewer standing behind sees as their right.

Now I'm moving to the key placement and shoulder/arm construction, writing a helper function that generates rib geometry cylinders along a chain of points, then thinking through typing concerns—using `any` for the chain parameter since the exact exported type is uncertain, which is acceptable for a one-off script.

For the arms, I'm planning to sweep a cylindrical skin along the arm chain so it inherits bone weights automatically, add a sphere for the elbow joint and a cuff for the wrist, and use a polyline path (rather than a smooth catmull curve) for the arm chain so joints stay sharp instead of getting rounded by the sweep.

Now I'm figuring out finger placement using direction vectors computed from the elbow-to-wrist vector, positioning a palm box oriented along a hand-direction vector relative to the arm's tip bone, and checking that the chain's tip reference works correctly given the number of joints versus spans in the arm.

Working out finger offsets...

Simplifying to explicit offset fractions for the pincer tips and thumb joints, then setting up finger sweep geometry with hexagonal caps and chain naming for parent-arm relationships.

Now building the leg chains with hip-knee-ankle joints per side, applying cylindrical sweeps and rib geometry along each leg segment.

Working on the sole paint for the dark underside plus the foot outline polygon points, making sure the shape stays convex and doesn't self-intersect.

I'm connecting the leg tube to the ankle with a smoothing band at the correct radius and height to cover the seam, double-checking the z-ranges so the heel region aligns properly with the leg origin. Adding small toe rivet details before moving on to the head.

Now for the head, I'm laying out the upper head plate and jaw as separate beveled boxes positioned so their edges slightly overlap for a clean joint, then placing a lathe-generated dome on top sized to fit within the head's width and depth, checking proportions against the head's half-width and half-depth.

For the eyes, I'm placing a chrome bezel cylinder, an amber glowing sphere lens flattened along the z-axis, and a small circular pupil plane positioned just in front of the lens's protruding tip, calculating the exact z-offset so the pupil sits flush against the curved front of the lens.

Now I'm figuring out the brows—two small angled bars above each eye to give a friendlier expression, working through how to tilt them properly using the plate's extrude thickness direction rather than a rotation parameter.

Placing the brow boxes near the head top, then working out teeth and jaw grille geometry: positioning a small teeth decal plane just below the head bottom edge, and sizing the grille plane at the jaw front to match a 90x26 texture ratio scaled to 0.09 wide.

Now I'm checking that the mouth sits properly beneath the eyes, confirming the teeth strip aligns right under the eye bottoms. For the ears, I'm laying out a yellow bezel cylinder along the x-axis, a dark silver disc cylinder slightly further out, and an ear decal plane at the outermost position, making sure each piece embeds correctly into the head's half-width without poking through.

Now I'm placing the antenna: a short base cylinder, a coiled gold wire sweeping upward, a glowing red ball on top, and a thin core rod running through the coil, keeping it straight rather than tilted, with the total height working out to about 0.444. I'm also adding four yellow rivet bolts at the front corners of the head for detail, then moving on to plan the neck, dome, shoulders, and finally the belt plate dimensions.

Placing the rivets around the shoulder edge using trig positions in a ring, 6 per side with radius .022, 12 total, then considering the stem connection between torso and shoulder at the torso's half-width.

Checking the gap between torso and shoulder for a connecting cylinder, then plotting the arm tube's sweep points from shoulder joint through elbow to wrist, verifying it clears the hip/belt region. Now I'm starting the key assembly, defining a lathed boss profile for its geometry.

Still placing overlay layers...

Scaling the key outline up to 1.2x and sizing its wings against the torso width confirms good proportions, and checking the floor contact points for the feet keeps them within tolerance. Now I'm moving to writing the actual SVG markup for the panel, starting with the viewBox and background rect.

Writing panel SVG...

Still writing SVG details...

Still writing texture code...

Now I'm verifying all nine texture components are accounted for, then tallying up the total part count across torso, head, shoulders, and arms to make sure the model stays manageable.

Checking frame inheritance and the remaining API signatures — lathe, extrude, sweep, coil, and glow all take color/bone options consistently, and glow works fine on parts with either textures or plain colors.

For the ear cylinder, I'm placing it with a direction vector so the geometry's y-axis aims along the given direction, attached to the head bone. Now I'm working out the ribbed neck lathe profile, generating a radius sequence at incrementing heights to create a segmented look.

Still writing lathe profile...

Now I'm working out the small accessory pieces: lamp bezels on the chest, and I'm nudging the back and front panel plane offsets slightly to avoid z-fighting with the torso surface, settling on small millimeter-scale gaps before placing the main panel plate.

Next I'm adding corner rivets to the panel plate, but deciding to skip them since the panel SVG already has dots drawn in. For the side tabs and vents, I'm setting up a helper to raycast against the torso surface to find hit points, then using those hits to place decals with orientation taken from the surface normal.

Then I'm positioning small yellow box tabs embedded into the torso at specific side heights, oriented so their thin axis aligns with the surface normal. Writing paint function for belt...

Setting up arm chains for both sides...

Adding the cuff cylinder, finger placement checks, and verifying palm/finger geometry alignment with the body; also setting up key joints and bone naming for rivets.

Checking that the plate extrusion and bevel work correctly on small shapes, especially the head plate and key bow's rounded lobe outline — I want to make sure the smoothing doesn't cause self-intersection at the concave waist, so I'm considering dialing smoothing down to be safe.

Setting smoothing to 1 and a small bevel for the key, then moving into writing the actual build code — defining the builder setup with naming and paint resolution, plus a helper function to generate a star-shaped polygon by alternating outer and inner radius points around a circle.

Now I'm naming the finger joints (fingerA, fingerB, thumb) to keep them unique, placing the hip ball joint in red at the top of the leg, and planning the rib segments along the legs while skipping the region near the knee joint.

Extending that same rib-segment approach to the arms with similar spacing, then setting the tube and rib radii for legs versus arms, and double-checking the foot outline extrusion and wall orientation before writing out the full component with correct bone rotations for the brow and teeth.

For the antenna I'm adding a thin golden rod attached to the head bone, then wrapping a coiled sweep around it using a small radius and low-poly sides for a metallic look.
